Pediatric Ankle Fractures
Background/Epidemiology
Ankle fractures represent approximately 5% of all pediatric fractures and 15% to 20% of all
physeal injuries.1-4

Pediatric ankle fractures are the most common physeal fractures of the lower extremity and
the third most common fractures overall, behind distal radius and finger fractures.5
Transitional fractures are a unique subset of pediatric ankle fractures that represent ankle
injuries during various stages of physeal closure.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Physeal considerations
Distal tibia and fibula epiphyses appear at approximately ages 6 months and 2 years,
respectively. The medial malleolus appears at approximately age 7 or 8 years.6
The characteristic pattern of physeal closure over a 2-year period is responsible for
transitional fracture patterns in adolescents.
Growth plate closes centrally, followed by medially, followed by posterolaterally, followed
by anterolaterally.
The distal fibula physis closes approximately 1 to 2 years after the distal tibia.
The distal tibia contributes 3 to 4 mm of growth per year and just less than 50% of growth of
the tibia.
Fractures typically occur through the hypertrophic zone of the growth plate.
Ligaments are primary stabilizers of the ankle joint and, in children, and are stronger than
the physis itself.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Knowledge of the biology of the physis is critical in the evaluation and management of
pediatric ankle fractures. Injury patterns and outcomes are largely related to injury to
the physis and physicians’ ability to restore anatomy and growth potential. The distal
tibia epiphysis appears at approximately age 6 months, and the fibular epiphysis follows
at approximately age 2 years. At approximately age 7 years, the medial malleolus
becomes visible. Although injuries to the ankle are less common in younger children,
these injuries may be more difficult to detect on radiographs.6 Injuries in children tend
to travel through the physis more often because it is weaker than the surrounding bone
and ligamentous structures.

As children approach maturity, the pattern of closure of the distal tibia physis leads to
characteristic fracture patterns classified as transitional fractures. The distal tibia physis
closes over an 18-month to 2-year period, beginning at approximately age 12 years in
girls and age 14 years in boys but can occur at any time between ages 10 and 19 years.
The fibular physis closes approximately 1 to 2 years after the tibial physis. The distal tibia
physis closes in a characteristic pattern beginning centrally. The physis then
progressively closes first medially, then moving back laterally, starting posteriorly
followed by the anterolateral portion (Figure 1). This last portion to close, the
anterolateral portion, is the attachment site for the anterior inferior tibiofibular
ligament. This attachment site is referred to as the Chaput tubercle. This anatomy is
responsible for the characteristic juvenile Tillaux fracture, one of the transitional fracture
patterns.
Figure 1 Illustrations show asymmetric closure (shaded area, arrow) of the pediatric
distal tibia physis over approximately 1.5 years. (Adapted with permission from Mac
Nealy GA, Rogers LF, Hernandez R, Poznanski AK: Injuries of the distal tibial epiphysis:
Systematic radiograph evaluation. AJR Am J Rad Roentgenol 1982;138[4]:683-689.)
A child’s ankle is stabilized primarily by the deep fibers of the deltoid medially and the
talofibular and calcaneofibular ligaments laterally (Figure 2). These ligaments attach to
the epiphyseal portion of the bone and provide no protection to rotational or
translational forces across the physis. Fractures typically occur at the hypertrophic zone
of the growth plate. The hypertrophic zone is characterized by larger chondrocytes and
less matrix, which makes it relatively weaker than other areas. The reserve zone is the

location at which the progenitor cells of the growth plate reside.7,8 Fractures that cross
this reserve zone theoretically increase the risk of growth arrest.
Figure 2 Lateral and medial view illustrations show the lateral ligaments of the ankle,
which include the syndesmotic ligaments and the lateral ligamentous complex. The
syndesmotic ligaments include the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament, the posterior
inferior tibiofibular ligament, and the interosseous ligament (not shown). The lateral
ligamentous complex includes the anterior and posterior talofibular ligaments and the
calcaneofibular ligament. The anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament and posterior inferior
tibiofibular ligament connect the distal fibula metaphysis with the lateral tibial epiphysis,
and the calcaneofibular ligament connects the distal fibula epiphysis with the lateral
aspect of the calcaneus. The medial ligamentous structures include the superficial
deltoid ligament, which connects the medial malleolus to the medial calcaneus and the
medial aspect of the navicular, and the deep deltoid ligament, which connects the medial
malleolus to the talus. (Reproduced with permission from Blackburn EW, Aronsson DD,
Rubright JH, Lisle JW: Ankle fractures in children. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2012;94[13]:1234-
1244.)
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Rotational forces are most commonly responsible for injuries to the ankle in children.
Inversion ankle injuries in children typically result in distal fibula physeal fractures.
External rotation is more likely to lead to transitional fractures, which occur during distal tibia
physeal closure.

Ankle fractures most often are caused by rotational forces on the ankle and are
associated with a wide range of severity depending on the energy placed across the
ankle. Inversion injuries are the most common type and often result in distal fibula
fractures. Historically, these injuries were thought to involve the distal fibula physis
because the calcaneofibular ligament attaches below the physis and is stronger than the
physis above. Many of these injuries are difficult to visualize on radiographs and require
targeted examination to assess. This dogma has been challenged recently with MRI
studies, which have noted fewer injuries to the physis and more ligamentous
involvement than previously thought.9
Transitional fractures are a unique subset of ankle fractures in adolescents that result
from external rotation injury to the ankle. The distal tibia physis closes over a nearly 2-
year period, beginning at approximately age 12 years in girls and age 14 years in boys. It
uniquely closes centrally first, progressing medially before moving laterally. Because of
the pattern of physeal closure, portions of the growth plate that are open remain
susceptible to injury. Triplane fractures occur earlier in the progression and can be
classified as Salter-Harris type IV injuries because they involve metaphyseal and
epiphyseal fracture lines. Typically, the metaphyseal portion is observed on lateral
radiographs, whereas the epiphyseal portion is observed on AP radiographs (Figures 3
and 4). This pattern result from the stronger closed physis resisting injury and energy
transferring into the metaphysis. The location and size of the Thurston-Holland fragment
is affected by the severity of injury, stage of closure, and force across the ankle. Multiple
variants of triplane fractures are possible, including two- to five-part patterns and extra-
articular fractures (Figures 5 and 6), which involve fractures through the medial
malleolus.10,11

Tillaux fractures occur in children 1 to 2 years older than children with triplane patterns;
however, the specific age depends on the patient’s skeletal maturity. These are Salter-
Harris type III injuries, and the Tillaux fragment is characteristically the anterolateral
portion of the epiphysis. The mechanism of injury is thought to be more of a supination–
external rotation injury and an avulsion of the anterolateral epiphysis because of the
anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (Figures 7 and 8). With the anterolateral portion of
the epiphysis being the last to close, it is at risk during this small window between
closure of other portions of the physis and skeletal maturity. After closure of the physis,
ligamentous injuries, such as syndesmotic injuries, are more likely to occur. The anterior
inferior tibiofibular ligament is a portion of the syndesmosis, and in higher energy
injuries in children, a Tillaux fragment may indicate a more severe injury. Providers
should evaluate imaging studies carefully for medial widening or other fractures.12,13

In very young patients with injuries about the ankle, especially those not yet walking
independently, providers must maintain a high index of suspicion for nonaccidental
trauma. The rotational mechanism is the same; however, characteristic imaging findings
more suggestive of nonaccidental trauma are metaphyseal corner fractures14 (Figure 9).
Figure 9 AP radiograph of both legs of a 25-day-old newborn boy who presented with
multiple sites of skin bruising and lethargy, which was obtained as part of a skeletal
survey for possible nonaccidental trauma, demonstrates bilateral bucket-handle
fractures (arrows) at the distal tibiae. The fractures are at different stages of healing. A
callus (arrowhead) surrounds the left distal tibia. This fracture configuration is
characteristic of nonaccidental trauma. (Reproduced with permission from Chaturvedi A,
Mann L, Cain U, Chaturvedi A, Klionsky NB: Acute fractures and dislocations of the ankle
and foot in children. Radiographics 2020;40[3]:754-774.)

The Salter-Harris classification is the most used classification system and is based on a
description of the fracture relative to the physis15 (Figure 10).

Ankle injuries have been classified in various manners in children. Typically, the Salter-
Harris classification system is used and describes the fracture and its relationship with
the physis. This classification system is descriptive and may indicate risk to the growth
plate. Salter-Harris type I and type II fractures are extra-articular and are purely physeal
or involve a metaphyseal fragment (Thurston-Holland fragment), respectively (Figure
12). Salter-Harris type III and type IV fractures have a fracture line through the physis and
into the articular surface. Type III fractures break through the physis and exit through
the epiphysis, whereas type IV fractures transfer energy through the metaphysis and
epiphysis. Type V fractures are considered a compression-type injury to the physis.
Injuries usually are through the hypertrophic zone of the growth plate and potentially
preserve the reserve zone, which contains the progenitor cells.7,8 Salter-Harris type III
and type IV injuries cross the physis and increase the risk to the physis. This is evident
with fractures involving the medial malleolus because these fractures can occur in
younger children and involve the more cartilaginous portion of the distal tibia.17,18
Figure 12 Sagittal CT scan shows a Thurston-Holland fragment (arrow). This fracture
fragment is the metaphyseal portion of Salter-Harris type II and type IV fractures.
(Courtesy of Julia Sanders, MD, Denver, CO, and Aaron Brandt, MD, Denver, CO.)

The adult classification systems based on mechanism of injury, such as Lauge-Hansen
classification system, have been used for pediatric patients; however, given the
differences in anatomy and the lower risk to the syndesmosis in children, they have
lower utility in this patient population. The Dias-Tachdjian classification system is used
more often in children and is similar to the Lauge-Hansen classification in describing the
position of the foot and the force applied. Injuries are classified as supination–inversion,
supination–plantar flexion, supination–external rotation, and pronation/eversion–
external rotation. The real value of this classification system is that it can provide
providers an understanding of the mechanism of injury and the manner in which to
reduce the fracture during mangaement.16 This classification system has not been
proven to predict outcomes in most studies; however, Binkley et al19 noted a higher risk
of growth disturbance in patients with pronation/eversion–external rotation patterns.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
Age of patient, activity, and reported mechanism of injury are important factors that increase
suspicion of ankle injury. Rotational mechanisms of injury may lead to tibial injuries in younger
children but more likely will involve the ankle as the child ages.
Physical examination is critical because nondisplaced injuries are more difficult to visualize on
imaging studies but still require appropriate management to prevent complications. Careful
inspection of the foot and ankle and palpation of the physes, bones, and ligaments will guide
additional workup.
The physical examination should include palpation along the syndesmosis and the proximal
tibia and fibula and the foot to ensure that associated injuries are identified.
Imaging Studies
Radiographs are used to evaluate injury but may be of lower utility in younger children or
those with nondisplaced injuries; AP/lateral/mortise views and AP/lateral views of the tibia
typically are ordered.
CT should be considered for any articular fracture and may aid in characterization and
targeted management.

MRI can be performed in patients with an occult fracture or for ligamentous evaluation but is
not routinely obtained during acute evaluation because it is costly, time-consuming, and
unlikely to affect management.

Imaging Studies
Evaluation of ankle injuries may be a challenge. Ankle pain may be caused by many
etiologies, including trauma, overuse injury, infection, rheumatologic conditions, and
oncologic processes. Providers should be diligent in the evaluation of patients with ankle
pain, with or without trauma to ensure findings are not missed. Imaging studies in
children may be a challenge given the radiolucent cartilaginous portion of bone, which
makes the physical examination critical in detecting the injury and guiding other
diagnostic tests. CT is valuable in its ability to provide a more detailed evaluation of
bone, especially in patients with articular fractures and injuries more difficult to
characterize via radiography (eg, transitional fractures, which include fractures in
multiple planes). CT scans may help surgeons with characterization and may increase
the accuracy of reduction and fixation; however, the overall effect on treatment
outcomes is not well described.20 MRI also may be of some use but often is avoided
because of the cost and difficulty of performing such imaging studies in children. MRIs
are particularly useful in the detection of ligamentous injuries, occult fractures, and
growth arrest down the line. MRI is most important in evaluating for other causes of
ankle pain, such as osteomyelitis (Figure 13). In addition, Petit et al21 reviewed 29 ankle
fractures to evaluate the accuracy of the radiographic description compared with MRI
and noted that only one of the fractures was incorrectly described based on
radiographs. Other studies have shown no effect on management, which tips the cost-
benefit scale away from the routine use of MRI.21,22

Management
Principles
Restoration of normal anatomy
Anatomic reduction of articular injuries
Protection of the physis to minimize the risk of a growth disturbance
Nonsurgical Management
Nondisplaced fractures are managed via immobilization and weight-bearing modifications
depending on the location of injury and patient age.
Patients with a displaced fracture should undergo reduction and repeat imaging studies to
evaluate the need for surgical treatment. Residual displacement should be no more than 3
mm, and a low threshold should be maintained for CT if any concerns exist.
Transitional fractures may be managed via reduction and cast immobilization; however,
displaced Tillaux fractures may be difficult to reduce. CT should be performed after closed

Nonsurgical Management
Most injuries can be managed nonsurgically. Nondisplaced fractures can be managed via
immobilization, with the type of immobilization dependent on the injury and patient
factors. Distal fibula fractures typically are Salter-Harris type I or type II injuries and are
unlikely to displace without concomitant tibial fracture or other injury. These fractures
can be managed via a short leg cast or a walking boot; if a child has no other injuries,
these fractures often can be managed via full–weight bearing. If a tibial fracture present,
this fracture typically guides management, including weight-bearing restrictions and
surgical decision making. Nondisplaced tibia fractures can be managed nonsurgically;
however, most providers recommend non–weight bearing for 4 to 6 weeks.
Displaced fractures about the ankle should be initially managed via closed reduction.
The goal of closed reduction is to restore the normal anatomy. If the provider can reduce
the fracture with an acceptable alignment, the fracture can be managed nonsurgically
via cast immobilization and a 4- to 6-week period of non–weight bearing. Reduction of
displaced fractures is performed following the same principles as those for any fracture,
including re-creation of deformity and opposite positioning in a cast or splint. Any
reduction attempt requires adequate analgesia and adequate assistance. Because these
injuries involve the physis, reduction should be performed with care to minimize
additional injury to the physis. No more than two to three attempts should be made to
reduce these injuries because each attempt poses a potential risk to the physis, and
difficulty reducing the fracture suggests a soft-tissue block.3,23,24 Fractures that cannot
be reduced after two to three appropriate attempts should be managed surgically. The
Dias-Tachdjian classification system can be used to help guide reduction. Transitional

Surgical Management
Surgical management depends on numerous factors, including fracture pattern, displacement,
and residual displacement after reduction.
General surgical principles include restoring the articular surface and physis and minimizing
fixation across the physis.
Fractures with residual displacement greater than 2 to 3 mm after attempted reduction
should be managed surgically.
Medial malleolus fractures are most commonly Salter-Harris type III or type IV injuries and
are associated with a higher risk of nonunion and growth-related complications.

Surgical Management
Surgical management of pediatric ankle injuries is necessary if closed techniques cannot
adequately restore normal anatomy. The distal tibia physis contributes approximately 3
to 4 mm of length per year in children. Distal tibia physeal injuries are associated with a
relatively high rate of growth-related complications (as high as 65%).23 Given this high
rate of complications, surgical management plays a larger role in the management of
these injuries. Most studies support 3 mm as the cutoff value for surgical
management4,11,23-26 (Figure 14). Salter-Harris type III and type IV injuries and medial
malleolus fractures are associated with a higher risk for growth disturbance, and the
threshold for surgical management, whether closed or open, should be lower.17,18 Many
studies have suggested that most of this risk likely results from the injury pattern and
mechanism of injury; however, factors such as residual displacement at the articular
surface and the physis affect outcomes.5,27,28

Closed and open reduction techniques have been used with success in pediatric ankle
fractures. In these injuries, the provider should attempt to reduce and maintain
alignment of the fracture as much as possible. If fixation must cross the physis, implants
such as smooth Kirschner wires (K-wires) are less likely to harm the growth plate.
Outcomes are similar between closed versus open techniques and between smooth wire
versus cannulated screw fixation given that the surgeon can attain appropriate
reduction.29-31 As children approach maturity, physeal sparing techniques become less
important. Therefore, transitional fractures can be managed via fixation across the
physis, and the most important facture goal is anatomic reduction of the articular
surface (Figure 15). Lurie et al32 investigated adolescent ankle fracture outcomes in 67
patients and noted that a fracture gap of more than 2 mm, residual displacement after
reduction, nonsurgical management, and complications were most predictive of poor
outcomes.

Complications
Complications related to pediatric ankle injuries include growth-related complications, such as
growth arrest causing longitudinal or angular deformity; posttraumatic arthritis; chronic pain;
and compartment syndrome.
The rate of growth arrest has been reported to be as high as 65%. Higher rates have been
reported in fractures with a residual gap greater than 3mm; Salter-Harris type III and type IV
injuries; medial malleolus fractures; and higher energy injuries, which usually occur with
increased displacement.

Talar fractures typically result from a forced dorsiflexion mechanism of injury with an

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management is indicated for nondisplaced talar neck and body fractures; closed
reduction should be attempted for displaced fractures; however, if the physician is unable to
attain anatomic reduction, surgical management is indicated.
Talar neck fractures usually result from dorsiflexion mechanisms of injury and may be most
stable in plantar flexion.
Immobilization and non–weight bearing are necessary to prevent displacement. Weight
bearing is not recommended until radiographic healing is present.
Surgical Management
Surgical indications are not well defined; however, as patients approach skeletal maturity,
adult indications are used given the relative risk of osteonecrosis after these injuries.
Displaced fractures, especially those through the talar neck, should be managed via open,
anatomic reduction.
Closed surgical techniques can be successfully performed f the fracture is amenable (simple
fracture line, anatomic reduction).
Lateral process fractures should be managed via fragment excision versus ORIF depending on
the fragment size.

Surgical Management
Surgical management of talar fractures focuses on restoring anatomy and preventing
the risk of future complications, such as osteonecrosis and posttraumatic arthritis. In
children, fractures usually are less complex; however, as children approach maturity,
more adult type fracture patterns may be observed. Given the risk of osteonecrosis and
the limitations in radiographic evaluation, some surgeons advocate for fixation of all
talar neck fractures, especially in older children. More complex fracture patterns typically
result in increased fracture displacement, joint dislocations, and medial comminution.
Increasing displacement increases the risk for complications, such as osteonecrosis.
Therefore, anatomic reduction and restoration of length of the medial column of the
foot are paramount. An important principle in the management of these injuries is

Osteonecrosis is a major concern with any displaced fracture through the talar neck because

Higher energy injuries and displacement increase the risk for complications, such as

Chronic pain is the most common complication after talar neck and body fractures given the
likelihood of intra-articular involvement and/or secondary changes related to osteonecrosis.

Calcaneal Fractures
Background/Epidemiology
Similar to talar fractures, pediatric calcaneal fractures are extremely rare injuries, accounting
for less than 0.15% of pediatric foot fractures.6,52
75% of calcaneal fractures in younger children are extra-articular, and most do not necessitate
surgical management.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Injuries of the calcaneus in children typically are less severe than those in adults and result
from a lower energy impact. This usually is attributed to the primarily cartilaginous makeup of
the calcaneus during childhood and the flexibility of the foot and resistance to fracture.56-58
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Pediatric calcaneus fractures more often result from lower energy mechanisms of injury and
result in nondisplaced or minimally displaced injury patterns.
Higher energy calcaneus fractures in children are caused by a fall from a height or a
substantial axial load.
Surgeons should always evaluate for other injuries related to the mechanism of injury;
however, spinal fractures are less commonly associated with calcaneal fractures than other
extremity injuries.6

Other Tarsal Fractures
Background/Epidemiology
Because of the complex anatomy of the midfoot, injuries to this region result in many patterns
and may cause variable amounts of disability. These fractures may range from avulsions to
comminuted open injuries and often are associated with soft-tissue injury.
Fractures of the cuboid, navicular, and cuneiform represent approximately 2% to 7% of all
pediatric foot fractures.
The most common fractures to the midfoot are avulsion fractures of the navicular and cuboid.
These generally are low-energy injuries, which may be managed via a walking cast for 2 to 3
weeks.
Displaced fractures of the navicular, cuneiforms, and cuboid generally are high-energy injuries,
with high rates of associated injuries. ORIF generally is required.
Anatomy and Biomechanics

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The midfoot consists of five bones—the navicular; the cuboid; and the medial, middle,
and lateral cuneiforms—and their associated joints. These bones generally ossify within
the first 4 years of life, beginning with the cuboid and ending with the navicular.
Interestingly, ossification centers are not always symmetric within the cartilaginous
anlage.65
The midfoot is essential to maintaining the arch of the foot and providing range of
motion through inversion and eversion. The mobile lateral column allows for adaptation
to uneven surfaces, and the more rigid medial column provides support for push-off.

and the cuneiforms. This may result in simple fracture lines or more severe
comminution, and the diversity of fracture patterns identified suggests the complexity
and variety of forces and mechanisms of injuries that may cause these fractures.69

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The tarsometatarsal joint, also known as the Lisfranc joint, divides the forefoot and the

The tarsometatarsal joint is a complex structure of bony and ligamentous structures. The
bases of the first three metatarsals are trapezoidal in shape, with the articulation of the

ligaments span from the second to fifth metatarsal bases. An oblique ligament runs from
the second metatarsal base to the medial cuneiform, with the interosseous and plantar

Physical examination should focus on signs of instability at the tarsometatarsal joint. Common

Patient History and Physical Examination
Patients usually present with pain and swelling at the midfoot and inability to bear
weight. The patient history often includes a substantial fall or collision or a twisting
mechanism during sports activity. Plantar ecchymosis is nearly pathognomonic, and pain
with palpation of the midfoot and attempted forefoot pronation and abduction often are
present. As many as 30% of Lisfranc injuries may be missed in adults with multiple
traumatic injuries. Missed Lisfranc injuries in children may be compounded because of
incomplete ossification and the inability of children to communicate effectively. A careful
neurovascular examination should be performed and compartment syndrome should

No preferred treatment option has been established for the management of Lisfranc
injuries in the skeletally immature population. Management has largely hinged on
immobilization or closed reduction and percutaneous pin fixation.74 Nonsurgical
management may vary by patient age but should consist of immobilization and a period
of non–weight bearing. Initial cast immobilization with progression to weight bearing via
a walking cast or boot is most common. A bulky dressing or splint may be initially
required because of soft-tissue swelling. Interval radiographs to confirm stability should
be considered. A course of physical therapy should be considered, especially in athletes
returning to sports activity. Pure ligamentous injuries may require longer periods of
immobilization and non–weight bearing than bony injuries.
Surgical techniques have evolved over time and are similar for pediatric patients and
adults. Open reduction should be performed if closed reduction is unsuccessful because
mechanical blocks to reduction, including osteochondral fragments or chondral
avulsions, often are present. Various fixation methods has been described, including
external fixation, suspensory suture button fixation, and K-wires and screws.75,76
Primary arthrodesis has been proposed in the adult literature, with similar outcomes at
midterm follow-up compared with plate or screw fixation.77,78 No studies have assessed
the result of this technique in pediatric patients, and additional research should be
performed before regular use of primary fusion in the skeletally immature patient
population.
The largest pediatric case series to date describes nonsurgical management of all purely
ligamentous injuries and surgical management of approximately 50% of fractures, all of
which were displaced. Eighty-nine percent of patients treated via open reduction
underwent screw fixation. Nonsurgical treatment was more likely in younger patients.
Non–weight bearing was substantially longer in older patients and those treated
surgically.79 Regardless of the technique, the goal of management should be
maintenance of anatomic alignment.
